passage: In the 1890s, one touring company performed the same melodrama in nearly every town it visited, while a rival troupe offered a new program almost every week. The first company's manager privately called the play "a tired old horse" and spent his energy commissioning new work, almost none of which lasted a season. Box-office ledgers show that the melodrama paid for those experiments year after year. Whatever the manager thought of it, the old play was the company's ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The ledgers show the same play reliably funding the company year after year, so it was the company's "staple," its dependable regular offering. "Triumph" would make the play a celebrated success, but the manager scorned it and its value lay in steady receipts, not acclaim. "Venture" describes a new, uncertain undertaking, which fits the manager's commissions, not a play performed unchanged for years. "Sequel" would require a follow-up to an earlier work, but the company performed one unchanged melodrama.
